`generate` turns the one-token step of <PageLink page="generation/sampling">Sampling</PageLink> into a longer text, by feeding each new token back in as input.

**This page has no backward pass.** `generate` calls `forward` only. It computes no loss and no gradient, and it changes no parameter. Every number here is an Illustrative Example, so no text generated by a trained model is shown.

<ConceptStep>Actual implementation</ConceptStep>

<CodeReference symbol="generate.generate" />

Reading it line by line:

- **The window.** `ids[-window:]` is the last `window` ids, or all of them if there are fewer (<CodeLine id="embed.generate-window" />). The list itself keeps every id, and the function returns all of them.
- **The last position only.** `forward` returns one row of logits for each position, and the loop uses only `logits[-1]` (<CodeLine id="generation.last-logits" />). The causal mask in attention (<CodeLine id="generation.mask" />) means an earlier position cannot read later tokens, so only the last row has read the whole window. That is the reason the comment on the line gives.
- **No reuse between steps.** Each step runs `forward` on the whole window again. The cache that `forward` returns is for the backward pass, and here it is discarded by `logits, _ =` (<CodeLine id="model.discard-cache-generate" />).
- **Positions follow the window.** `embed_forward` adds `pos_emb` rows from 0 up to the input length (<CodeLine id="generation.position" />). So the same token gets a different position row as the window slides, and row 0 always goes to the oldest token in the window.

## What train.py and talk.py pass

`generate` has two callers in the pipeline. Both pass the same window and sampling settings. They differ in the seed and in how many tokens they ask for.

| Argument         | `train.main`                                              | `talk.main`                                                             |
| ---------------- | --------------------------------------------------------- | ----------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `seed_ids`       | The first 3 ids of the first validation window            | The encoded prompt                                                      |
| `max_new_tokens` | The literal 30                                            | `config.max_new_tokens`, which is <ConfigValue name="max_new_tokens" /> |
| `window`         | `config.seq_len`, which is <ConfigValue name="seq_len" /> | `config.seq_len`, which is <ConfigValue name="seq_len" />               |
| `temperature`    | <ConfigValue name="temperature" />                        | <ConfigValue name="temperature" />                                      |
| `top_k`          | <ConfigValue name="top_k" />                              | <ConfigValue name="top_k" />                                            |
| `top_p`          | <ConfigValue name="top_p" />                              | <ConfigValue name="top_p" />                                            |
| `rng`            | The generator also used to shuffle batches                | Its own generator, kept across prompts                                  |

<CodeStep id="generation.train-seed" />

<CodeStep id="generation.train-call" />

<CodeStep id="talk.generate" />

The window is <ConfigValue name="seq_len" /> tokens, while the `pos_emb` table has <ConfigValue name="context_len" /> rows. `forward` asserts that its input fits the table (<CodeLine id="forward.assert" />). <PageLink page="mathematics/embeddings">Embeddings</PageLink> shows what this means for the rows past the window.

`train.main` shares one generator between sampling and batch shuffling, so printing a sample changes the next epoch's batch order. <PageLink page="training/training-loop">Training Loop</PageLink> covers this.

`talk.main` creates its generator once, before the prompt loop. So a second prompt does not restart the random sequence, while a new run of `talk.py` does.

## Defaults

These are the values in `config.py`. `top_k` is <ConfigValue name="top_k" />, so top-k is off by default. Greedy decoding is also off, because `temperature` is above the guard.

<SamplingDefaults />

## What the model is and is not

The model is a text continuation model. Given a list of token ids, it gives probabilities for the next token, and the loop extends the list one token at a time. `talk.py` describes itself the same way:

<CodeStep id="generation.talk-prompt" />

It is not an assistant. The code gives no basis for treating it as one:

- **No conversation.** Each prompt is encoded and generated from alone (<CodeLine id="talk.encode" />), so nothing from an earlier prompt reaches the model. The only thing that carries over is the generator's position.
- **No message format.** The vocabulary has `<unk>`, characters and merged tokens. It has no tokens that mark a speaker, a question or an answer.
- **No stopping.** The only limit is `max_new_tokens`, so the loop always appends exactly that many tokens. It can stop in the middle of a sentence.
- **Output is the continuation only.** `talk.py` prints just the new tokens (<CodeLine id="talk.print" />). A blank line quits (<CodeLine id="generation.talk-quit" />).

<PageLink page="reference/not-in-this-model">Not in This Model</PageLink> lists what the code does
not do.
